title: Descartes
keyWorks: Letters to Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia (1643–1649)
summary: Descartes was a French philosopher and mathematician who wanted to build knowledge on clear and distinct foundations. In his last book, The Passions of the Soul, he described in detail how feelings arise where body and soul meet, and how we can handle them wisely.
onEmotions: For Descartes, the “passions” are emotions of the soul caused by movements of the body (he called these “animal spirits” — the finest particles of the blood, running through the nerves). He counted six primary passions: wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness; all the others are combinations of these. The passions are not enemies of reason: they are good by nature, because they tell us what is useful or harmful and move us to act. The will cannot order a feeling to disappear, but it can gradually direct attention — and in this gentle, indirect way change the feeling itself.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a legitimate state: it shows that something matters to you and the outcome is unclear. Descartes described a closely related passion — “irresolution”: a kind of fear that holds the soul suspended between several possible actions and doesn’t let it choose any of them. According to Descartes, the body is already stirred up at such moments, and willpower alone can’t cancel that agitation. But you don’t have to wait for complete certainty. In the Discourse on Method he offers the rule of a traveller lost in a forest: don’t wander in circles, but walk as straight as you can in one direction — that way you will at least come out somewhere. Anxiety doesn’t have to vanish at once because of this, but it stops being a dead end. You can let it stay beside you and still take one small step of your own choosing.
anxiety.practice: Write down one small action you would consider reasonable right now, even without complete certainty. You can simply note: “I choose this step, and for now that’s enough.”

fear.text: Fear is an ancient and honest signal: the body gets ready to protect you before you’ve had time to think. That is how Descartes understood it: as a passion in which the soul is inclined to believe that what it wants will not come about, while the body is already prepared for flight. One important idea of his: the will cannot simply order fear to leave. But it can turn attention to other considerations — to reasons why the danger is smaller than it seems, to the fact that you have strength and support. Feeling responds not to commands but to what we hold before the mind’s eye. Descartes also advised not making important decisions at the peak of agitation, but letting the “animal spirits” — the storm in the body — settle a little. You can acknowledge fear, listen to it, and still not hand it the wheel.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly is frightening me right now — and what one reason or memory tells me I’ve already coped with something similar? Keep your attention on it for a minute.

sadness.text: Sadness needs no justification. For Descartes, sadness is one of the six primary passions — part of the very make-up of a human being. He described it as an unpleasant languor of the soul when it senses some lack or harm, and he believed it has a purpose: it warns us of what is not good for us. His observation about the “inner emotions of the soul” is interesting: we can feel sadness and at the same time a quiet satisfaction — as when we read a sad story or watch a tragedy in the theatre. Sadness and a deep agreement with yourself don’t exclude each other. So you don’t have to push sadness away: you can let it be, and notice that somewhere beneath it you remain yourself — someone capable of feeling deeply.
sadness.practice: Imagine your sadness is a scene in a book about you. As a caring reader, what would you feel toward this character?

quote.text: They are all good by nature, and we have nothing to avoid but their misuse or their excess.
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.source: The Passions of the Soul, art. 211

grief.text: Grief is the price of love, and it has the right to last a long time. Descartes, who valued reason so highly, did not demand that people be unfeeling. When a friend of his lost a brother, Descartes wrote to him that he was not one of those who think tears and sadness unworthy of a man and that one must keep dry eyes. He himself lived through the death of his little daughter Francine and, by all accounts, grieved for her deeply. In his theory, sadness is the natural movement of the soul when it loses what it has joined itself to in love. Reason is not there to forbid the pain but, over time, to gently turn attention to other things as well: to what was lived together, to what goes on living in you. To grieve is not weakness but faithfulness.
grief.practice: Recall one specific detail about the person or thing you’ve lost — a gesture, a phrase, a smell. Let it simply stay with you, without hurrying either tears or comfort.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts because human beings are built for connection. Descartes defined love as the movement by which the soul, of its own will, joins itself to what seems good to it — so that it begins to regard itself and what it loves as parts of one whole. Loneliness, if we think in these terms, is the feeling of having become “a part without a whole.” Yet Descartes himself deliberately lived in solitude in Holland for many years, and wrote that among busy people one can live as quietly as in a desert. For him it mattered to distinguish: solitude chosen for the sake of thought and a lack of love are different things. You could say that your longing for connection is not a defect but proof that your capacity to join with the world is alive in you.
loneliness.practice: Name one being, place or activity with which you feel “part of one whole,” even just a little. What could you do today to touch that connection for a minute?

anger.text: Anger is a living feeling, and it often points to a real injustice. Descartes described anger as a particular kind of hatred toward those who, as it seems to us, have done us harm, joined to a desire to respond. He distinguished two kinds of anger: one flares up quickly and quickly passes — it is found in people who are good at heart; the other hides inside and gnaws for a long time. Descartes considered the best remedy for excessive anger to be “generosity” (générosité) — a calm self-esteem grounded in your firm resolve to use your free will as well as you can. A generous person doesn’t believe that someone else’s wrongdoing can take away what matters most. Then anger can be acknowledged, you can hear what it tells you about your boundaries — and not let it decide for you.
anger.practice: Finish the sentence: “My anger is telling me that what matters to me is…”. Separately, note what in this situation truly depends on your own decision.

shame.text: Shame is one of the most painful feelings, and to feel it is to be a human among humans. Descartes defined shame as a kind of sadness grounded in self-love and in the opinion or fear that we are blamed. He didn’t consider shame useless: together with its opposite, “glory,” shame spurs us to strive for what is worthy. But Descartes warned of something else too: other people’s opinion is an unreliable measure, since people often misjudge. A more reliable support lies in what depends on you: in your resolve to act as you yourself judge best. You can listen to shame as a signal — “it matters to me how I’m seen” — and then ask yourself more calmly: and what do I myself think about this?
shame.practice: On a sheet of paper, separate two things: “what I think others thought of me” and “what I myself think of what I did.” See how far they coincide.

guilt.text: Guilt tells you that you care what your action was like. Descartes called the related passions “repentance” and “remorse.” Repentance is a bitter sadness at the thought that we have done something bad; remorse is an uneasy doubt about whether what we are doing is good. Descartes considered them useful when an action really is bad — they help us make amends. But in his letters to Princess Elisabeth he added an important consolation: if we acted as we sincerely thought best at the time, we have no reason to condemn ourselves, even if the outcome was bad. We answer for good will and honest judgement, not for omniscience. Guilt can be turned from a verdict into a guide for the future.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: “Given what I knew and felt then, did I act according to my best judgement?” And then: “What can I do or understand now?”

envy.text: Almost everyone feels envy, though it’s hard to admit. Descartes described it as a kind of sadness mixed with hatred, when we see a good fall to someone we consider unworthy of it. He honestly distinguished this passion from just indignation: sometimes behind envy there is a real sense of injustice. Descartes observed that there is least envy in “generous” people — those who value above all not external goods but their own firm intention to live well, which no one can take from them. From this point of view, envy is a clue: it shows what you really desire. There’s no need to be ashamed of it; you can decode it and bring your attention back to what depends on you.
envy.practice: Write down exactly what the person you envy has. And then — what desire of your own lies behind this, and what small step toward it is open to you.

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are neither laziness nor vice; sometimes the soul simply stops responding. For Descartes, the passions are what move the soul to want things and to act; when they are almost absent, the world seems flat. Descartes has no separate chapter on apathy, but from the standpoint of his theory you could say: the way into the life of feeling begins with the very first passion — wonder. It is a simple movement of attention toward something new or unusual, before any judgement of “good” or “bad.” Wonder requires neither strength nor enthusiasm: it is enough to notice. Descartes would probably advise not forcing yourself to be joyful, but gently letting your attention rest on something small and unfamiliar — from there the soul can gradually begin to come back to life.
emptiness.practice: Find one thing around you that you haven’t noticed before: a little crack, a shadow, a shade of colour. Just look at it for a minute, expecting nothing.

confusion.text: Confusion is a normal state when the old answers have stopped working. Descartes knew it from the inside: his philosophy began with the decision to doubt everything he had previously believed. For him, doubt was not a defeat but the beginning of clarity. He set out simple rules of method, one of which is especially useful in confusion: divide the difficulty into parts and move from the simplest to the more complex. And until things became clear, he proposed a “provisional morality” — living by reasonable rules without waiting for final answers. Your confusion, from this point of view, is a moment of honesty: you see that the old picture is incomplete. It doesn’t need to be fixed immediately; it’s enough to find one small clear part.
confusion.practice: Break what’s confusing you into three or four separate questions. Choose the simplest one and answer only that.

quote.text: To divide each of the difficulties I examined into as many parts as possible and as may be required in order to resolve them better.
quote.author: René Descartes

fatigue.text: Tiredness is not a sign of weakness but the honest response of body and soul to strain. Descartes, for all his fame as a thinker, confessed to Princess Elisabeth that he gave very few hours a day to intense thought, and the rest of his time to rest and simple things. When Elisabeth suffered from exhaustion and sadness, he advised her to let her mind rest: to imitate those who, looking at the green of a forest, the colours of flowers or the flight of birds, think of nothing in particular. For Descartes, soul and body are closely bound together, and an exhausted body finds it hard to sustain clear thought. Allowing yourself rest is not running away from your duties but part of a reasonable life. Your tiredness has a right to be heard.
fatigue.practice: For a minute or two, look at something living — a tree, the sky, a plant on the windowsill — trying not to reason about anything, just looking.

boredom.text: Boredom is a familiar feeling, and there’s nothing shameful in it. Descartes described a similar passion — satiety (disgust): a sadness that comes from the very thing that used to delight us. We are made in such a way, he says, that most goods are good for us only for a time, and then they begin to weigh on us. So boredom is a natural signal: the old has run its course, and the soul is looking for something new. The opposite of boredom in Descartes can be taken to be wonder — the first of all the passions, a lively response to what seems new and unusual to us. Wonder doesn’t have to wait for adventures: it is possible toward the familiar too, if you look at it more closely. Boredom, from this point of view, is not empty time but an invitation to learn again how to wonder.
boredom.practice: Take the most ordinary object near you and ask three questions about it that you don’t know the answer to. Which of them makes you even a little curious?

quote.text: Wonder is the first of all the passions.
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.source: The Passions of the Soul, art. 53

joy.text: Joy is a beautiful feeling, and there is no need either to justify it or to fear it. Descartes defined joy as a pleasant emotion of the soul in which its enjoyment of a good consists. He was no ascetic: for him the passions are the source of the sweetest moments of life, and the more vividly a person feels, the more joy they are able to taste. Descartes also distinguished “intellectual joy” — the quiet satisfaction that comes when we understand something or act in keeping with our convictions. Such joy is especially lasting because it depends less on circumstances. Let yourself notice what exactly is making you glad right now, and don’t hurry on to the next task: for Descartes, knowing how to enjoy a good is part of wisdom.
joy.practice: Stay with this joy for a minute: where do you feel it in your body? Name, out loud or to yourself, exactly what you’re glad about.

quote.text: The people whom the passions can move most are capable of tasting the most sweetness in this life.
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.source: The Passions of the Soul, art. 212

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the deepest feelings open to a human being. Descartes defined love as an emotion of the soul that moves it to join itself willingly to what seems good to it. The key point in this definition: we begin to see ourselves and the one we love as parts of a single whole. That is why, he explained, in true love we are ready to care for the other as for the better part of that whole. Descartes distinguished shades of love by how we esteem the beloved: affection, friendship, devotion. Tenderness, from this point of view, is the natural expression of this feeling of unity. There’s no need to be shy about it or to hide it behind irony: love, for Descartes, is one of those passions that are good by their very nature.
love.practice: Think of someone you feel tenderness for. In one sentence, how would you describe the “whole” you feel yourself part of together with them?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling that connects us with others. Descartes called it “gratitude” (reconnaissance) and defined it as a kind of love aroused in us by the action of someone who has done us good, or at least wished to. Notice: for Descartes, what matters is not only the good itself but the other person’s good intention. He considered gratitude a virtue that binds people together, and ingratitude one of the bitterest vices. From this point of view, gratitude is neither a duty nor politeness but a natural movement of a soul that notices it has been cared for. You can simply live it: notice who has done you good and how, and let the feeling warm you.
gratitude.practice: Recall someone’s good intention toward you — even if things didn’t entirely work out for them. What do you feel when you think of it?

hope.text: Hope is one of the most human of feelings. Descartes defined it as a disposition of the soul to believe that what it desires will come about, and observed that hope almost always lives next door to fear: the more strongly we hope for something that doesn’t depend on us, the more anxious we become. So in The Passions of the Soul he advised distinguishing what depends on us from what doesn’t. Where much is within our power, hope can become firm resolve. Where the outcome doesn’t depend on us, it is wiser to desire more calmly, accepting the course of things. This is not giving up hope but a way of making it steadier. Your hope is legitimate; the only question is what it can lean on so that it doesn’t rock you too hard.
hope.practice: Divide your hope into two parts: what in it depends on you and what doesn’t. For the first, write down one step; for the second, one word that will help you let go of control.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia joins tenderness and sadness, and there is nothing strange about it. Descartes described a similar passion — “regret”: a particular sadness with a bitter note, because it is bound up with the memory of a pleasure that cannot be brought back. He also understood well how the past lives in the body. In a letter to Chanut he told how as a child he had loved a girl who was slightly cross-eyed, and for a long time afterwards felt an inexplicable fondness for people with such a gaze — until he understood where it came from. Early impressions leave traces that come alive without our knowing. Understanding this doesn’t devalue the feeling: it makes nostalgia clearer and gentler, and turns the past into a source of self-knowledge.
nostalgia.practice: Think about which smell, sound or image makes you nostalgic. What in it mattered so much to you back then — and is there room for that quality in your life now?

craving.text: A craving is a strong and entirely real feeling: it’s as if the body has already decided for you, and “I want it right now” fills everything. Descartes described such moments very precisely. In The Passions of the Soul he wrote that in strong agitation everything the imagination presents tends to deceive the soul: the reasons in favour of the object of passion seem much stronger than they are, and the reasons against seem weaker. His main advice was not to defeat desire with a single effort of will — that, for Descartes, is impossible. He proposed something else: not to make a decision while the blood is stirred up, to turn your thoughts to something else, and to let time and rest calm the agitation. A craving is like a wave: it rises, crests and falls. You don’t need to argue with it; it’s enough not to hurry.
craving.practice: Tell yourself: “Right now I’m not deciding, I’m just waiting ten minutes.” Set a timer, keep your hands busy with something simple, and then see what the wave has become.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a flaw of character or proof of weakness. It is a cycle that took a long time to form, and it is hard for anyone to get out of. Descartes explained why: through habit, strong links form between movements of the body and thoughts of the soul, and they fire before we have time to think. But he also insisted that these links can gradually be rebuilt. He gave the example of dogs trained not to rush at game when they hear a gunshot, but instead to approach it calmly: if habit can be retrained even in animals, it is all the more within a human being’s reach. Descartes wrote that even the weakest souls can, over time, acquire mastery over their passions if they bring patience and skill to it. There is no place for shame here: there is long, careful work in which you can lean on other people.
addiction.practice: Notice one “link” in your cycle: a situation or time of day after which the craving usually appears. Just write it down — without reproach, as an observer.

hangover.text: The morning after is a hard time: your body aches, and anxiety, shame and fragments of last night are spinning in your head. All of this is very human. Descartes helps us see how closely body and soul are intertwined here. In The Passions of the Soul he observed that sadness or unease can arise simply from the state of the body, without any external cause — and then the soul looks for something to attach them to. So part of today’s gloom is the voice of an exhausted body, not a fair verdict on you. Descartes believed that memory is stored in traces that impressions leave in the brain; when the traces are blurred, the memory breaks off, and the imagination is quick to fill the gaps with the worst. You don’t have to believe all the dark thoughts of this morning at once. You’ll be able to sort things out calmly later, once your body has recovered.
hangover.practice: Put off going over last night for a few hours. Right now, do one thing for your body: drink some water, wash your face, open a window.

euphoria.text: A flash of euphoria is a vivid experience when everything seems possible, and there’s no need to be suspicious of it straight away. Descartes was no enemy of strong feelings: he held that the passions are good by nature and make life sweet. But in his letters to Princess Elisabeth he made a subtle remark: every passion shows its object as bigger than it is — the goods it promises seem greater and more solid than they will later turn out to be. This is not a reproach to joy but knowledge about its optics. Descartes suggested enjoying the good while keeping for reason the right to a calm assessment. You can live this high fully — and simply put off the big decisions it prompts for a day or two, until you can see which of them still hold.
euphoria.practice: Write the ideas and plans that came on the wave of this high into a separate list marked “come back in two days.” The rest of the time, just let yourself be glad.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high can be very painful: a moment ago everything was shining, and now the world is grey and heavy. This is a natural movement, and Descartes knew it from his own experience. In a letter to Elisabeth he recounted that as a child he was sickly and pale, and doctors predicted he would not live long. In his words, what set him right was largely that he trained himself to look at circumstances from the most favourable angle he could find, and to seek his chief satisfaction in what depended on himself. This is not a call to force yourself to be happy. For Descartes, feelings don’t obey orders, but attention can be gently turned — and the body gradually responds. The dip is a wave, not a new truth about your life.
crash.practice: Find one thing in today that is still all right, however small, and hold your attention on it for half a minute.

panic.text: A wave of panic is one of the most frightening experiences: your heart pounds, your breathing falters, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen. Descartes described how a passion seizes the body: the “animal spirits,” as he called the finest particles of the blood, set the heart and muscles in motion, and this agitation lasts as long as its cause does. He honestly acknowledged that the will cannot stop this movement with a single command. But it can refuse to follow it — not run, not take drastic steps — and wait until the storm in the body settles. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Your task right now is not to handle it “correctly” but simply to wait it out, leaning on what is around you.
panic.practice: Put both feet flat on the floor and feel the support beneath you. Make your exhale longer than your inhale — several times in a row — and silently name five objects you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is it all for,” the sense of an abyss and of finitude — visits many thoughtful people, and there is nothing shameful in it. Descartes, too, asked himself the most radical questions. When Princess Elisabeth asked him what could sustain a person in life, he named several truths, among them the thought of the vastness of the universe and of the fact that each of us is part of a larger whole: a family, a society, the world. For Descartes this didn’t diminish a person but freed them: not everything rests on your shoulders alone, and you are woven into something bigger. He was a believer, and part of his support lay in faith; but even outside it there remains what he called “wonder” — the capacity to marvel at the world, and not only to be terrified by it.
dread.practice: Name three connections that make you part of something bigger: a person, a place, a pursuit. You can simply write down their names.

fomo.text: Almost everyone knows the fear of missing out: it feels as if real life is happening somewhere else, and you’re in the wrong place. Descartes, if anything, made the opposite choice. He left noisy Paris and lived for many years in Holland, often changing address so he could think in peace. As his motto he chose a line from Ovid: “He who has hidden well has lived well.” In The Passions of the Soul he advised distinguishing desires whose fulfilment depends on us from those that don’t: the latter, he wrote, grow especially easily and torment us, because they can be neither fulfilled nor let go. The fear of missing out usually belongs to this second kind. You can acknowledge it — and bring some of your attention back to where your life is actually happening.
fomo.practice: Write down one “it’s more interesting over there” and next to it one “here, now, I have…”. Look at the second a little longer.

sleepless.text: Three in the morning is when thoughts seem louder and darker than by day, and this is a very understandable state. Descartes thought a lot about how the body and the imagination affect each other. According to his theory, when the body is tired and agitated, the same traces come alive in the brain again and again, and thought goes round in circles. He warned: while such agitation lasts, it’s better not to trust the imagination or make decisions — you need to wait until time and rest calm it. Descartes himself valued sleep and rest highly, and advised Princess Elisabeth, who suffered from heavy thoughts, to let her mind rest on simple and pleasant images. Night-time conclusions needn’t be taken seriously — morning usually revises them.
sleepless.practice: Say to the thought: “I’ll consider you in the morning.” Then picture one peaceful place in detail — its colours, sounds, the temperature of the air.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only your relationship with a person but also the sense that the world can be trusted. Descartes knew what it is like to discover deception. His philosophy begins with his noticing that his senses had sometimes deceived him, and that it is prudent never to trust completely those who have deceived us even once. But what matters is what came next: Descartes did not give up on the world. He doubted, re-examined the foundations — and gradually, step by step, told apart what could be relied on from what could not. He also wrote of “indignation” as a natural reaction to undeserved harm. Your pain is legitimate. And over time trust can be rebuilt, without giving up the caution this experience has taught you.
betrayal.practice: Write down one thing or one person you can still rely on. This is your first “certain” point after doubt.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing because love and the fear of losing are intertwined in it. That is how Descartes defined it: as a kind of fear bound up with the desire to keep possession of some good. He noticed that the strength of jealousy depends less on the weight of the reasons than on how highly we value that good — which is why even a small cause can set off a storm. Descartes considered such a passion understandable when something truly valuable is at stake. But he also noted that excessive jealousy often speaks not only of the other person but also of our own lack of confidence in ourselves. This observation doesn’t accuse — it helps you see that jealousy also contains a request to yourself: to remember your own worth.
jealousy.practice: Divide a sheet into two parts: “what I know for sure” and “what I’m assuming.” See which part is bigger right now.

resentment.text: An old grievance is a heavy burden, and you carry it not because you want to but because you really were hurt. Descartes treated hatred as a passion that has its causes, but he pointed out one peculiarity of it: hatred, unlike love, is never without sadness, and even in small doses it harms the person who feels it. In other words, resentment weighs most on the one who carries it. Letting it go, from this point of view, is neither a gift to the person who hurt you nor an admission that nothing happened, but a way of caring for yourself. Descartes advised not ordering a feeling to vanish, but gradually shifting attention to what is dear to you. Resentment may fade slowly — and that’s normal.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself: “How much room does this grievance take up in my day?” and “What would I like to give at least part of that room to?” Write down the answer.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it is understandable. Descartes defined love as an emotion by which the soul joins itself to the beloved so that the two come to feel like parts of one whole. When a relationship ends, that whole seems to be torn apart, and the pain feels almost physical. Descartes didn’t demand that you “pull yourself together” at such a moment. His advice is gentler: the will cannot order a feeling to leave, but it can gradually change what we hold before the mind’s eye. Feelings respond to the images they are usually linked with — so by little by little bringing your attention back to your own affairs, people and pursuits, you give your heart something new to lean on. This is not forgetting but a slow rebuilding of a whole.
heartbreak.practice: Name one activity or one person that belongs only to your own life, not to the relationship that has ended. Give it a few minutes today.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out at any moment is felt by a great many capable people, and it doesn’t prove you are where you are by accident. Descartes opens the Discourse on Method with a sentence about good sense being the most fairly distributed thing among people, and immediately admits that he never considered his mind more perfect than other people’s. The most famous thinker of his time made no claim to being exceptional: he said only that he had been lucky enough to find a good path. His idea of “generosity” is especially useful here: genuine self-respect, for Descartes, rests not on the certainty that you are better than everyone else but on the firm intention to do conscientiously what you judge to be right. No one can expose that intention — it really is yours.
impostor.practice: Write down one thing you do conscientiously, regardless of how “brilliant” it looks.

quote.text: Good sense is the best distributed thing in the world.
quote.author: René Descartes

self_hatred.text: When the inner critic tells you that you are bad, it hurts a great deal, and its voice can sound convincing. But Descartes drew an important distinction that helps you not agree with that voice. He called genuine humility a virtue: an honest acknowledgement that weakness and error are part of human nature — without placing yourself above or below others. But the sense of your own worthlessness, which drains you of strength and resolve, he called “vicious humility” — a distortion, not the truth. The real foundation of self-esteem, for Descartes, is single and open to everyone: free will and the intention to use it as well as you can. Neither mistakes, nor others’ judgements, nor the harshness of the inner critic can cancel it.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one phrase your inner critic uses, and beneath it how an honest but kind person would say the same thing.

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything is a heavy experience, and it is often tied to real circumstances rather than to your weakness. Descartes knew well that much does not depend on us. That is why one of the rules he chose for himself while searching for truth reads: try to master yourself rather than fortune, and change your desires rather than the order of the world. He explained that only our thoughts and decisions are entirely within our power. This is not a call to resign yourself to everything. Rather, it is a way of getting your footing back: when the outside world won’t yield, there remains how you relate to what is happening and what small step you choose. Where it seems nothing can be done, usually one thing can.
helplessness.practice: Divide the situation into two columns: “not in my power” and “in my power.” In the second, write at least one very small thing.

quote.text: My third maxim was always to try to master myself rather than fortune, and to change my desires rather than the order of the world.
quote.author: René Descartes

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is a familiar state, and it rarely has much to do with laziness. Descartes described a related passion — “irresolution”: when the soul weighs its options for so long that the time for action passes. He noticed that those most prone to it are people who very much want to do the right thing and are afraid of making a mistake. The remedy, for Descartes, is to get used to forming definite judgements and to consider that you have done your duty if you did what you judged best, even if it later turns out you were wrong. Perfection is not a condition for beginning. You can allow yourself a first step that doesn’t have to be the best one — as long as it is taken. Descartes himself built his method out of simple steps, not out of one stroke of genius.
procrastination.practice: Choose the very first action, almost laughably small — open the file, write one heading — and do only that.

uprooted.text: Being torn from home is a deep experience: the familiar ground disappears, and you seem a stranger even to yourself. Descartes knew life far from his homeland: he lived in Holland for more than twenty years, often moving. The Discourse on Method has an image that fits such a time very well. When you rebuild your house, he wrote, you need to provide yourself in the meantime with other lodgings where you can live comfortably. That is why he drew up a “provisional morality” for himself — a few simple rules for living sensibly while the main thing was still under construction. A move is like such a rebuilding: the old way of life has been taken apart, and the new one hasn’t come together yet. You don’t have to demand of yourself that you feel at home straight away — you can set up temporary but sound lodgings for the soul.
uprooted.practice: Write down two or three simple rules or rituals that will help you live steadily through this transition — for example, one familiar walk, or a call to people close to you.

overload.text: Overload from an endless feed and informational noise is a real strain, not a whim. Descartes, though he lived long before smartphones, formulated a rule that sounds very modern today. In the Rules for the Direction of the Mind he wrote that whoever tries to take in many objects at a single glance sees none of them distinctly. Just as a craftsman doing fine work fixes his eyes on one point, so the mind must be directed to one thing, simple and clear. Descartes considered attention the chief instrument of thinking — and it can be protected. Your weariness with the noise is, from this point of view, the natural response of a mind being made to look in every direction at once. It needs one point.
overload.practice: Close everything except one window or one thing in front of you. For a minute look only at it, noting its details.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real is frightening and disorienting. Descartes described something similar in the Meditations: he admitted that in dreams he had sometimes seen himself sitting by the fire, dressed — and could find no reliable sign to tell dreaming from waking. But from this doubt he drew something that cannot be shaken: since I doubt and think, I exist. Even if everything seems unsteady, the one who notices it is there. And in the last of the Meditations Descartes added that the soul is joined to the body not as a pilot to his ship but in the closest possible way: pain, hunger, warmth are direct signs of that union. You can return to them.
unreality.practice: Clench and unclench your fists, and feel the temperature of your palms. Say to yourself: “I notice this — so I am here.”

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling. For Descartes it is connected with “wonder,” which he considered the first of all the passions: a sudden surprise of the soul that makes it attend closely to whatever seems extraordinary to it. He noted a particular feature of wonder: it doesn’t yet judge whether the thing is good or bad — it simply opens our eyes. Descartes considered it useful because wonder makes us remember and learn what we did not know before. He warned only against a kind of stupefaction, when astonishment keeps us from looking further. So your awe needs neither explaining nor hurrying: it is the very moment when the world has become new again. You can simply stay in it and look.
awe.practice: Try to remember one specific detail of what filled you with awe — a colour, a sound, a line. You can write it down in a single word.

relief.text: Relief is a warm and well-earned feeling: tension lets go and the body exhales of its own accord. Descartes described a similar transition: when hope becomes so strong that fear disappears, it turns into “confidence,” and the soul grows calm. He also noticed that joy resonates through the whole body — the heart beats more evenly, and warmth seems to spread through the veins. From Descartes’ point of view, you could say that relief is the moment when soul and body both stop bracing for the worst. Don’t rush to look for the next thing to worry about. Descartes considered knowing how to enjoy a good part of wisdom, and relief is a good too — worth living fully rather than skimming past.
relief.practice: Notice where in your body something has let go — shoulders, jaw, breathing. Take one slow exhale and let that place relax a little more.

calm.text: Calm is a state worth noticing and protecting. Descartes wrote about it in his letters to Princess Elisabeth. He distinguished good fortune, which depends on external things, from what he called contentment of mind — an inner peace that depends on us. To reach it, according to Descartes, three things are enough: to try as well as you can to understand what you ought to do; to hold firmly to your decision; and not to desire what is not in your power. Such calm doesn’t require everything around you to be perfect. It is more like being in agreement with yourself. If you feel it now, it is neither chance nor a lull before the storm, but the fruit of something in you that is already well ordered.
calm.practice: Note what helped you arrive at this calm just now. Write it down in one line — it will come in handy on another day.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful state when thoughts fall into place by themselves and you want to act. Descartes had his own famous moment. According to his account, which has come down to us through his first biographer, in the winter of 1619, after spending a day alone in a heated room, he experienced an exaltation, and that night he had three dreams after which he felt he had found the foundations of a “wonderful science.” That inspiration shaped his life. But Descartes was not content with a single flash: in the years that followed he patiently tested and built up what had been revealed to him then, according to the clear rules of his method. Inspiration, from this point of view, is a beginning worth respecting and, at the same time, carefully transferring to paper. Let it be — and write it down while it’s alive.
inspiration.practice: Write down the main idea of your inspiration in a sentence or two, and add one first step from which you could start testing it.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is unpleasant to admit, but Descartes described it calmly, like a naturalist. In The Passions of the Soul he calls “derision” a particular joy mixed with hatred: it arises when we see a small misfortune befall someone we think deserves it. And he adds a remarkably subtle observation: those most inclined to such joy are people with some noticeable defect or who have suffered public humiliation — they want to see others in the same unenviable position. This is not an accusation but a clue: schadenfreude often grows out of one’s own wound. Descartes believed that any passion can be handled wisely once we understand where it comes from. Instead of punishing yourself, you can ask: what in me is hurting so much right now that someone else’s failure brings relief?
schadenfreude.practice: Name one vulnerability of your own that this person’s story touched. Treat it the way you would treat a friend’s pain.

contempt.text: Contempt gives a sense of superiority, but it rarely brings peace. Descartes linked contempt with wonder: it is the movement of the soul by which we note a thing’s smallness, just as by esteem we note its greatness. Importantly, he turned the question from others back to ourselves. The only thing that gives us legitimate grounds for esteeming ourselves, according to Descartes, is how we use our free will. A person who understands this — a state Descartes called “generosity” (générosité) — readily recognizes that everyone else has the same free will. That is why, he wrote, the generous despise no one. From this point of view, contempt is a sign that we are measuring people by something external: status, intelligence, success. You can notice this without shame and ask yourself what your own dignity rests on.
contempt.practice: Think of someone you feel contempt for, and try to name one choice they made while trying to act as they thought best.

disgust.text: Disgust is instant and bodily: you want to recoil. Descartes believed the passions prepare the body for action even before reflection, and disgust is a good example. He also made an interesting observation: some people have strange aversions — someone can’t bear the smell of roses or the presence of a cat — and Descartes supposed these were traces of impressions from early childhood, when the body had been strongly affected by something similar. So our disgust is often linked to long-ago events rather than to what is in front of us now. Descartes also described another kind of it — “satiety” (dégoût), a sadness born of the very thing that once delighted us, when there is too much of it. Understanding what kind of disgust yours is is already a step toward freedom from it. This applies to disgust with yourself as well: it too may be an old imprint rather than the truth.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself: what does this disgust resemble? When did I first feel something like it? Write down whatever comes, without analysing.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is an understandable response to pain that has been inflicted. Descartes described anger as a kind of hatred toward those who have done us harm, joined to a desire for revenge, and he didn’t pretend the feeling was unworthy of a human being. His main practical advice applied to all strong passions: don’t make decisions until the agitation has settled. Passion, he wrote, makes the reasons in its favour seem far more convincing than they are, and makes the pleasure of revenge especially vivid. It’s better to suspend judgement and meanwhile consider the reasons on the other side. Revenge also quietly hands the offender power over your life: you keep responding to their move. You can listen to the wish for revenge as a signal — “I was treated unjustly” — and then, in calm, decide for yourself what kind of justice you need.
revenge.practice: Write down: what did the person who hurt me take from me, and what — my decisions, my values, my freedom — have I kept?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those closest to you is especially tormenting: first the flare-up, then the shame. Descartes distinguished two kinds of anger. One flares up quickly and visibly but does little and easily subsides. The other is barely visible at first but gnaws at the heart more and is more dangerous. And he wrote that those most subject to the first kind are people with a great deal of goodness and love in them. This doesn’t justify harsh words, but it is an important consolation: being quick-tempered with loved ones doesn’t at all prove there is no love — rather the opposite: where there is much attachment, there is much that can be hurt. Descartes didn’t advise ordering a passion to vanish: the will can’t do that. It’s better to shift your attention and let the agitation in the body settle. Then you can come back to the conversation — as someone who loves.
anger_at_loved.practice: When you feel yourself boiling over with someone close, say “I need five minutes” and go into another room. Come back when your breathing has steadied.

ambivalence.text: Loving and not being able to stand the same person at once is a very common state, and it makes it easy to decide something is wrong with you. Descartes could help ease part of that fear. In The Passions of the Soul he argued against the idea that two warring souls live within us. The soul is one, he wrote; the “struggle” we feel is a clash between the movements of the body that produce the passions and our will. Moreover, almost all feelings, for Descartes, are mixtures of the six primary passions: wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness. A mixed feeling toward someone close is not a split personality but a natural combination. You don’t have to choose one and renounce the other. You can distinguish which actions and memories feed the love and which feed the dislike, and decide how to act by leaning on what you judge best.
ambivalence.practice: On a sheet of paper, mark which of the six primary passions you feel toward this person right now. Look at this mixture as a portrait, not as a problem.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a loved one’s departure, a breakup or a long illness is often mixed with grief — and with shame about that relief. Descartes knew such a combination was possible. He distinguished passions that arise from movements of the body from “inner emotions,” which arise in the soul itself and can go their own way. In The Passions of the Soul he gives the example of a husband mourning his dead wife: his heart is gripped by sadness, while in the depths of his soul he may feel a secret joy. Descartes doesn’t condemn him: he simply shows that different voices can sound in us at once. Your relief doesn’t cancel your love and grief. It speaks of how hard things were for you, and of strength that is beginning to return. Both feelings can be acknowledged as real.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: “It hurts — and it’s easier. Both are true at once.” Write down what exactly has become easier and what it cost you.

indifference.text: Sometimes there is quiet inside where you are “supposed” to feel something — and that is frightening. Descartes offered a calm explanation. According to his theory, the passions arise where soul and body meet and depend on the state of the body — on what he called the “animal spirits.” When the body is exhausted, overloaded or has lived under strain for a long time, the response can become muted. Descartes also stressed that the will cannot directly summon or cancel a passion. Ordering yourself to “feel!” is as useless as ordering yourself not to be afraid. Indifference, from this point of view, is not a moral void but a state that deserves attention rather than judgement. Descartes advised acting indirectly: directing attention to what is usually connected with the feeling in question — and letting the body rest. Feeling often returns once there is room for it.
indifference.practice: Instead of demanding feelings of yourself, recall one specific detail connected with this event or person, and simply stay with it for a minute.

escape.text: Descartes himself knew the wish to drop everything. After finishing his studies, he decided to seek knowledge only within himself and in “the great book of the world” — and for many years he travelled, served in armies, observed. Later he left France for the Netherlands in order to live in peace and concentration. So Descartes would not have considered the urge to change your circumstances a weakness. But there is an important detail in his story: he went not only “away from” but also “toward” — toward his work, toward quiet for thinking. His method teaches us to divide a difficulty into parts. The wish to escape can be taken apart too: what exactly is draining you, what are you missing, what part of this could change without drastic steps? The dream of escape is a valuable message about your needs, and it deserves a careful reading.
escape.practice: Divide a sheet into two parts: “what I want to get away from” and “what I want to get to.” Fill in the second column with at least three words.

quote.text: Resolving to seek no knowledge other than that which could be found in myself or else in the great book of the world, I spent the rest of my youth travelling.
quote.author: René Descartes

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” can be bewildering: where does it come from, and what does it mean? Descartes left a remarkably candid testimony. In a letter to his friend Chanut he told how as a child he had loved a girl who was slightly cross-eyed, and for a long time afterwards noticed he was drawn to people with the same gaze — until he understood where it came from. Once he grasped the cause, the attraction stopped governing him. Descartes concluded: we are often drawn to someone because of a resemblance to old impressions we ourselves don’t remember. This is neither a moral judgement nor advice on what to do. It is an invitation to curiosity: the feeling is strong, but it has a history. By understanding what in your past or in your needs this person is answering to, you gain more freedom.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: whom or what does this person remind me of? Which of their qualities answers to something long familiar? Write down the first thing that comes.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgement is familiar even to great minds. The young Descartes wrote in his notes: just as actors put on a mask so that the blush of shame won’t show on their faces, so he, stepping onto the stage of the world where until then he had only been a spectator, comes forward masked. He knew this embarrassment well. Later, in The Passions of the Soul, Descartes explained that the will cannot simply order a passion to disappear, but it can direct attention: when we are occupied with the aim and meaning of what we are doing, agitation gradually loses its force. From this point of view, you don’t have to stop feeling nervous first in order to be among people. You can be nervous — and still act, leaning on what depends on you: your intention, your task, your interest in the person in front of you.
social_anxiety.practice: Before meeting people, choose one thing you’re going there for — to find something out, to say something, to help. During the meeting, gently bring your attention back to it.

quote.text: Larvatus prodeo — I come forward masked.
quote.author: René Descartes

uncertainty.text: When it’s unclear what will happen, it’s hard to commit to anything at all. Descartes called this state “irresolution” and considered it a kind of fear. He also offered what is probably its best-known remedy. In the Discourse on Method he compared himself to a traveller lost in a forest: such a traveller shouldn’t wander this way and that, still less stand still — better to walk as straight as possible in one direction, even if the choice was almost random. That way he will at least come out somewhere, which is better than staying in the middle of the forest. Descartes added: if you acted as you judged best, you have done your duty, even if it later turns out you were wrong. The uncertainty doesn’t vanish, but you gain a footing — not in knowing the future, but in your own decision.
uncertainty.practice: Choose one small direction for the coming week — not for your whole life. Write it down and agree with yourself to revisit the decision only after seven days.

quote.text: My second maxim was to be as firm and decisive in my actions as I could, and to follow even the most doubtful opinions, once I had adopted them, with no less constancy than if they had been quite certain.
quote.author: René Descartes

waiting.text: Waiting for an answer, for results, for news is exhausting: thoughts keep returning to what is no longer in our hands. Descartes believed the main mistake here is confusing desires whose fulfilment depends only on us with those that don’t. The first we can fulfil; the second, he wrote, are not worth desiring too ardently, or they only torment us. Hope and fear, as he described them, are two faces of one desire, wavering between possible outcomes. While waiting, it helps to do what Descartes advised: acknowledge that you have already done your part, and bring your attention back to what can be done now. This is not indifference to the result. It is a way of not handing your whole life over to the waiting while it lasts.
waiting.practice: Write: “My part is done: …” — and list what you’ve already done. Then choose one thing for today that has nothing to do with the waiting.

regret.text: Regret about the past can go round endlessly: “if only I had…”. Descartes considered repentance a useful passion if it helps us do better, but he also saw the danger — tormenting yourself where nothing can be changed anymore. He proposed a simple and profound rule. If at the time you acted as, so far as you could judge, was best, you did your duty, even if the result turned out badly. In his words, it was precisely this rule that freed him from the repentance and remorse that usually trouble weak and wavering minds. An error of judgement is not the same as ill will. From this point of view, it’s worth asking not “why did it turn out this way?” but “was I doing what I then thought best?” — and if so, lifting part of the blame from yourself.
regret.practice: Describe the decision you regret in two sentences: what I knew then, and what I thought was best. Look at them as the testimony of an honest witness.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is bitter and at the same time full of warmth. In The Passions of the Soul Descartes singled out a special feeling, called in French regret: a sadness with a particular bitterness, because mixed into it is always the memory of the pleasure that closeness gave, and the impossibility of having it back now. He observed precisely that the bitterness of longing is made of something good — of what once was. Descartes held that all the passions are good by nature, and only their excesses and our clumsy handling of them are bad. You don’t have to drive longing away — it is enough not to let it block out everything else. The memory that hurts now also holds what you love. By turning your attention to gratitude for it, and not only to the emptiness, you change the colour of the feeling without betraying it.
longing.practice: Write down one memory of this person that you’re grateful for. Let yourself feel both the bitterness and the warmth at once.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — hard news, war, injustice — is natural for a sensitive person. Descartes described pity as a sadness mixed with love or goodwill toward those who suffer undeservedly. He noticed that those most prone to pity are people who feel weak: another’s misfortune reminds them the same could happen to them. But even the most generous, he wrote, are not without compassion; only their compassion contains no bitter helplessness and turns into a good wish to help. Here is a hint about how to carry this pain: distinguish what depends on you from what doesn’t. You cannot abolish a war or an injustice. But you can keep your goodwill alive, do some small real thing, and not let despair take your strength away.
world_pain.practice: Put the news aside for an hour. Choose one small kind action — for a specific person or cause — and do it today.

rejection.text: When we are rejected, it feels as if our whole worth has been rejected. Descartes defined love as a movement of the soul that moves it to join itself willingly to what seems good to it — to picture itself and the other as parts of one whole. When the other doesn’t want that whole, pain remains, and it is real. But Descartes offered a support that cannot be taken away. The only thing that gives us a legitimate right to esteem ourselves, he wrote, is how we use our free will. Looks, position, others’ recognition come and go; self-respect rests on them only shakily. That you wanted to join with another was a movement of your free soul, and its dignity has not been lessened by the refusal. The other person’s answer is their decision, not a verdict on you.
rejection.practice: Write down one decision you made in the past month for which you can respect yourself — regardless of how others responded to it.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned keeps you constantly on guard. Descartes described a related passion — jealousy in the broad sense: a kind of fear connected with the desire to keep some good for ourselves. In his observation, such fear grows not so much from real signs as from how highly we value that good and how little we believe we can hold on to it. Descartes advised dealing with fear not by ordering “don’t be afraid” but by working with attention: a passion is sustained by the impressions we dwell on. If your thoughts keep painting the scene of someone leaving, the feeling grows stronger. If you gently bring your attention back to what is actually there — to the person’s words and actions, to your own strengths — the fear gradually subsides. Your worth does not depend on whether someone stays by your side.
abandonment.practice: When the fear of being left washes over you, write down: what do I know for sure right now, and what am I only imagining? Mark at least one fact from the first list.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds painfully, and Descartes wouldn’t play that down. But his understanding of love offers unexpected support. He discussed two sides of love: the desire to possess, and “benevolence” — wishing good to the one you love. The first suffers from being unrequited. The second can live without an answer: you can still wish this person well, and that feeling remains yours; no one has taken it away. Descartes also believed that love for what is truly worthy brings joy in itself. At the same time he was a realist: passion is sustained by attention, and if you endlessly return to the image of the beloved, it will grow. You can gently give yourself breathing spaces — not to force yourself to fall out of love, but so that your heart isn’t occupied by the wound alone.
unrequited.practice: Put into words one kind wish for this person — without expecting any reply. Then do something good for yourself.

humiliation.text: Humiliation — being made smaller than you are — wounds very deeply. Descartes lived at a time when wounded honour was considered grounds for a duel, and he looked at this soberly. He wrote that “generosity” is the best remedy for the excesses of anger: the generous person sets little value on what others can take from them, and so the insults that drive others to fury touch them less. The point is not to “rise above it” and feel nothing. The point is to find where the boundary lies: others can affect your position, reputation, mood, but not your will to act as you judge right. Humiliating treatment speaks of the other person’s act. And what you do with it is yours.
humiliation.practice: Divide a sheet into two parts: “what can be taken from me” and “what can’t be taken.” Fill in the second part with at least three items.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be very painful, especially when it seems to be what you’re judged by. Descartes is known for sharply distinguishing thought from body, but in the Meditations he also writes something else: I am not merely present in my body as a pilot is in a ship, but am very closely joined to it and, as it were, form one whole with it. The body is not a foreign object but a part of you, the part through which you feel hunger, warmth, joy. Descartes also noted that ideas of beauty depend largely on impressions and habits, and so differ from person to person. He saw his own worth not in the qualities of the body but in how a person uses their will. From this point of view, you can stop grading your body and instead thank it for what it does.
body_shame.practice: Place your palm on your chest or belly and feel your breathing. Name one thing your body is doing for you right now — without judging how it looks.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, everything changes: strength, plans, mood. Descartes knew this first-hand — he had been in poor health since childhood — and in his letters to Princess Elisabeth, who was also often ill, he wrote a great deal about the connection between soul and body. According to his theory, soul and body are so closely joined that the states of one are reflected in the other: illness changes feelings, and heavy feelings tire the body. So irritability or sadness during illness is not your weakness. At the same time Descartes spoke to Elisabeth about the space that remains to the soul: you can choose what to dwell on and find small reasons for contentment, without pretending the pain isn’t there. This is not a treatment and not a substitute for medical help. It is a way of remaining yourself when your body won’t cooperate.
illness.practice: Today, choose one small pleasant thing available to you in your current state — a taste, a sound, light from the window — and give it your attention for a minute.

pride.text: Pride in what you’ve done is a legitimate and good feeling. Descartes considered rightful self-esteem the key to all the virtues and called it “generosity” (générosité): a person knows that the only thing truly belonging to them is the free disposal of their will, and feels in themselves a firm resolve to use it well. He distinguished this from vanity — a self-importance based on externals: wealth, others’ praise, chance success. Your pride is closer to the first if it contains the essential thing: this was my decision, my effort, my persistence. Descartes also wrote of a special satisfaction felt by those who consistently follow what they judge best — he called it peace of conscience. Allow yourself this feeling: it doesn’t puff you up, it strengthens you.
pride.practice: Write down not only the result but also three decisions that led to it. These are what rightfully belong to you.

melancholy.text: Gentle melancholy is a subtle feeling: there is sadness in it but no despair, and you may even find something pleasant in it. Descartes wouldn’t be surprised. He noticed that when we read about sad events in a book or see them on stage, we feel sadness — and at the same time pleasure that these feelings are being stirred in us. This pleasure he called “intellectual joy”: it belongs to the soul itself. So sadness and joy can coexist. Descartes held that all the passions are good by nature, and that people capable of feeling deeply can taste the most sweetness in life. Gentle melancholy is an example of such depth. It doesn’t need fixing: you can let it sound like music in a minor key, and notice what is preserved in it.
melancholy.practice: Stay in this state for a few minutes: put on some fitting music or look out of the window. Write down one thing this melancholy helps you see.
